title: Does Medicare Save Lives?
research_question: Does gaining near-universal health insurance coverage at a standard eligibility age affect the intensity of hospital treatment received by acutely ill patients and their subsequent mortality? Specifically, do the changes in insurance characteristics that occur when individuals turn 65 lead to measurable reductions in short- and medium-term death rates among severely ill emergency-room patients?
data_description: The analysis uses California hospital discharge records covering the universe of patients discharged from state-regulated hospitals between January 1, 1992 and December 31, 2002. Each record contains the patient's age in days at discharge, gender, race/ethnicity, zip code, primary admission diagnosis (ICD-9), planned/unplanned status, route of admission (ER vs. non-ER), primary insurance provider, length of stay, list charges, and procedures performed, along with a scrambled SSN used to link mortality records and track transfers. The unit of observation is a hospital admission. The authors construct a sample of roughly 425,000 'non-deferrable' admissions—diagnoses with statistically equal weekday and weekend ER admission rates. Supplementary descriptive evidence on insurance coverage comes from the 1999–2003 National Health Interview Surveys, and employment evidence from the 1992–2003 NHIS.
institutional_context: Medicare provides hospital insurance (Part A) for free, and physician coverage (Part B) for a modest premium, to nearly all U.S. residents starting on the first day of the month they turn 65. The age-65 threshold produces sharp changes in insurance: roughly 60 percentage-point increases in Medicare coverage, a fall in uninsurance from about 13% to 3%, a large rise in supplemental ('Medigap' or employer) coverage, and a sharp decline in managed-care enrollment as most enrollees choose traditional fee-for-service Medicare. Medicare also imposes fewer utilization restrictions than many private or Medicaid plans and, prior to 1998, reimbursed post-acute care (e.g., hospital-based skilled nursing facilities) on a generous cost basis. These insurance changes occur abruptly at 65 even though underlying health, retirement behavior, and recommended medical practice change little at that exact age, especially for patients arriving at emergency rooms with acute, life-threatening conditions.
